title: SpareTrain: Fault-Tolerant LLM Training via Low-Cost Dual Modular Redundancy
claim: Discarding intermediate activations and recomputing them in segments trades extra compute for lower memory during the backward pass.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right timeline, compute and memory lanes with colored segment boxes
description: Two stacked timeline diagrams compare training without and with activation checkpointing (AC). Each has a Forward column (green header) and a Backward column (blue header), with a Compute lane above a dashed line and a MEM lane below. Panel (a) shows forward blocks F1–F8 in light boxes, each writing an activation A0–A7 to memory. Backward blocks B8–B1 are black boxes that read those activations through vertical arrows. Panel (b) shows only A0, A4 and A5 kept in memory. Forward blocks are grouped into red AC Segment #1 and orange AC Segment #2. During backward, F6–F7 and F1–F3 are recomputed inside the colored boxes and feed B8–B6 and B4–B1. Colored italic labels mark each segment's backward pass. The eye goes first to the black B blocks and the colored segment boxes.
caption: Activation Checkpointing (AC)
abstract: Dual Modular Redundancy (DMR) is a highly effective mechanism for detecting silent data corruption (SDC)—a critical reliability concern in large language model (LLM) training—by executing each operation twice. However, its high computation overhead has prevented practical deployment at scale. In this paper, we present SpareTrain, an LLM training system that achieves complete DMR with minimal overhead by repurposing the activation checkpointing mechanism and exploiting idle GPU time. Evaluations on up to 32 H200 GPUs show that SpareTrain improves throughput by 12–35\% over naive DMR, corresponding to only 3–14\% overhead compared to unprotected training, while maintaining full DMR error detection capabilities.
